exercises.prompt: Implement frequency(arr), where arr is an array of numbers, so it returns an object counting how many times each number appears — frequency([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]) is {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 3}. Repeated values need not be adjacent. An empty array returns an empty object {}.
hints: Keep a running tally object and walk the array, bumping one key each step.
The first time you see a value there is no count yet, so counts[x] = (counts[x] || 0) + 1 starts it at 0 before adding 1.
Loop the array updating counts[x] = (counts[x] || 0) + 1, then return counts — the last test proves non-adjacent repeats still land in the same bucket.

exercises.prompt: Implement groupByParity(arr) so it splits arr's numbers into two buckets and returns {even: [...], odd: [...]}, each bucket holding the matching numbers in their original order. groupByParity([1, 2, 3, 4]) is {even: [2, 4], odd: [1, 3]}. Both keys are always present: an empty array returns {even: [], odd: []}.
hints: Start the result with both buckets already in place — { even: [], odd: [] } — so empty and all-one-parity inputs still return both keys.
Walk the numbers and push each into the right array: x % 2 === 0 chooses even, otherwise odd.
for (const x of arr) { if (x % 2 === 0) groups.even.push(x); else groups.odd.push(x) } then return groups — pushing preserves original order within each bucket.

exercises.prompt: Implement tallyChars(str) so it returns an object counting how many times each character appears in str — tallyChars('hello') is {h: 1, e: 1, l: 2, o: 1}. An empty string returns an empty object {}.
hints: A string can be walked one character at a time with for (const ch of str), just like an array.
It is the same frequency tally as counting numbers — the key is now a character: counts[ch] = (counts[ch] || 0) + 1.
Loop the characters updating counts[ch] = (counts[ch] || 0) + 1, then return counts; the empty string simply never enters the loop and returns {}.

exercises.prompt: Implement groupByFirstLetter(words), where words is an array of non-empty strings, so it groups the words into buckets keyed by their first letter, returning {letter: [words]}. groupByFirstLetter(['apple', 'ant', 'bee']) is {a: ['apple', 'ant'], b: ['bee']}. Only letters that actually occur become keys, and words keep their original order within each bucket. An empty array returns an empty object {}.
hints: The key for each word is its first character, word[0]; several words can share one bucket.
The first time a letter shows up its bucket does not exist yet — create it with an empty array, then push into it.
if (!(key in groups)) groups[key] = []  then  groups[key].push(word) — create-then-push is what lets a bucket hold more than one word.

exercises.prompt: Implement groupByLength(words), where words is an array of strings, so it groups the words into buckets keyed by their length, returning {length: [words]}. groupByLength(['a', 'bb', 'cc', 'ddd']) is {1: ['a'], 2: ['bb', 'cc'], 3: ['ddd']}. Only lengths that actually occur become keys, and words keep their original order within each bucket. An empty array returns an empty object {}.
hints: Same bucketing move as grouping by first letter, but the key is now a number: word.length.
Create the bucket the first time a length appears, then push the word into it.
const key = word.length; if (!(key in groups)) groups[key] = []; groups[key].push(word) — then return groups.
